summary: Far from Earth, advice from the ground arrives late or not at all, so a crew has to check its own health and act on its own. Untethered Health Monitor is a working, simulated prototype that turns body and cabin readings into action. It measures, judges each reading against stated limits, alerts the right people, gives each crew member a step, and keeps a problem open until new data shows recovery. It watches physiological signals (vital signs, sleep, mood and symptoms) and the external environment (cabin CO₂, temperature, humidity, radiation and the link to Earth). The same system runs a spacecraft mission and a Mars rover excursion, using NASA data in both. Crew, symptoms and faults are simulated and labelled. Medical officers make the health decisions: this is decision support, not a medical device.
details:
THE IDEA

When Earth cannot answer in time, the crew still needs to know what is wrong, who acts and whether it worked. The system runs one loop for every problem: measure, judge, alert, act, and re-check until the data shows recovery.

WHAT WE MONITOR

Physiological: heart rate, blood oxygen, blood pressure, body and skin temperature, sleep, mood, fatigue, stress and reported symptoms. External: cabin CO₂, temperature and humidity, radiation dose rate and accumulated dose, and the communication link to Earth. Every value shows its source and age, and missing data stays marked as missing.

WHEN AND HOW WE ALERT

Readings are judged against stated limits: NASA standards where they exist, medical references or project assumptions otherwise. Alerts are graded by severity. Each alert goes to the module where the problem is and to the people it concerns, on their watch, their tablet and the shared screens. A reading that looks unreliable is re-measured before it counts. When exposure points to a rising risk, the system schedules extra self-checks in advance.

HOW WE RESPOND

Written procedures become steps for named crew members, each with a reason. A step closes only when new data confirms it or the medical officer signs it off; a device reporting “success” is not enough. When the link to Earth is down, the crew carries on with onboard steps, messages queue until contact returns, and late advice from Earth is flagged if it no longer fits the situation.

SHOWN IN THE PROTOTYPE

On a spacecraft: a cabin CO₂ problem alerts the crew, a reading is re-measured after poor sensor contact, a restart reports success but the step stays open until CO₂ recovers, and a late reply from Earth is reviewed and declined. On Mars: a measured solar storm warns a two-person EVA team to return to the rover.

NASA DATA

NASA OSDR EDA provides the ISS cabin CO₂, temperature and humidity history before the scenario starts; the CO₂ problem itself is simulated. NASA RadLab provides Orion radiation background and the shape of a Curiosity MSL-RAD storm for the constructed spacecraft event. The Mars scenario replays Curiosity MSL-RAD measurements from the May 2024 storm unscaled, with only the clock shifted, along Curiosity’s route. Area radiation readings are not personal dose.
